lessons.title: Cold Infusions and Decoctions
lessons.body:
Cold infusions and decoctions are the simplest ways to pull medicine from plants. Use cold infusion for delicate parts: flowers, leaves, fresh herbs. Use decoction for tough parts: roots, bark, seeds, dried berries. In Africa, you already know these methods from making tea or boiling roots for medicine. Now we measure for skincare.

Cold infusion: Take 20g dried or 40g fresh plant material. Put in a clean glass jar. Add 250ml clean water (filtered or boiled and cooled). Cover. Leave at room temperature for 4â8 hours, or overnight. Strain through muslin cloth. Use within 2 days in the fridge. Example: hibiscus petals, lavender flowers, mint leaves. For a facial toner, mix 50ml cold infusion with 50ml witch hazel.

Decoction: Take 30g dried tough plant material. Put in a pot. Add 500ml water. Bring to a boil, then reduce heat and simmer for 20â30 minutes. Cover with a lid to trap steam. Let it cool. Strain. This makes a stronger liquid. Use within 3 days in the fridge. Example: ginger root, licorice root, neem bark, cinnamon bark. For a skin wash, use 100ml decoction in 1 litre warm water.

Tools you need: kitchen scale, measuring jug, stainless steel or enamel pot (not aluminium), glass jars, muslin cloth or clean cotton cloth, funnel, airtight bottles. Always label with plant name and date. If you see mould, throw it away. For longer storage, freeze in ice cube trays and use one cube per session. In hot climates, keep everything cool and dark. These water-based extracts are gentle but spoil fast. Make small batches weekly. You can combine cold infusion and decoction: for example, a toner with hibiscus cold infusion and a small amount of ginger decoction for stimulation.

lessons.title: Oil Infusions: Solar and Heat Methods
lessons.body:
Oil infusions capture fat-soluble plant compounds. They are the base for salves, balms, massage oils, and facial serums. In Africa, you have abundant oils: coconut, palm kernel, shea nut, baobab, moringa, sesame, groundnut. Choose a stable oil like coconut or shea for long shelf life. For solar infusion, use dried plant material only. Fresh herbs contain water and will cause mould. Dry your herbs in shade for 3â7 days until brittle.

Solar method: Fill a clean glass jar halfway with dried herb. Cover completely with oil, leaving 2cm oil above the herb. Stir to remove air bubbles. Seal and place in a sunny window or outdoors for 2â4 weeks. Shake daily. Strain through muslin, squeeze well. Bottle in dark glass. Label. Shelf life: 6â12 months if kept cool and dark. Example: 100g dried calendula flowers in 500ml coconut oil. For a skin balm, use 50ml infused oil with 10g beeswax.

Heat method (faster): Use a double boiler or a glass bowl over a pot of water. Put herb and oil in the bowl. Heat water to 60â70Â°C (not boiling). Keep for 2â4 hours, stirring occasionally. Strain. This method is faster but can degrade delicate compounds. Use for roots, barks, and harder herbs. Example: 50g dried neem leaves in 250ml sesame oil. Heat for 3 hours. Strain. Use within 6 months.

Important: Never use direct high heat. Never use aluminium. For solar infusion in very hot climates, place jar in partial shade to avoid overheating. Test for rancidity: smell the oil. If it smells like crayons or old nuts, discard. For a richer extract, repeat the process with fresh herb in the same oil (double infusion). Always label with plant, oil, and date. These oils are excellent for African skin: shea and baobab are non-comedogenic and healing.

lessons.title: Tinctures and Glycerites
lessons.body:
Tinctures use alcohol to extract a wide range of plant compounds. Glycerites use vegetable glycerin for a sweet, alcohol-free option. Both are concentrated and last 1â3 years. In Africa, you can buy strong alcohol like vodka (40% or higher) or use local spirits like waragi, kachasu, or ogogoro if they are at least 40% alcohol. For glycerites, use food-grade vegetable glycerin.

Tincture method: Use a 1:5 ratio for dried herbs (1 part herb to 5 parts alcohol by weight). For fresh herbs, use 1:2. Example: 50g dried hibiscus in 250ml vodka. Put in a glass jar. Seal. Shake daily for 4â6 weeks. Strain through muslin. Squeeze. Bottle in dark glass with dropper. Dosage for skincare: add 5â10 drops to 30ml carrier oil or cream. For a facial toner, mix 10ml tincture with 90ml water. Shelf life: 2â3 years.

Glycerite method: Use a 1:4 ratio for dried herbs (1 part herb to 4 parts glycerin). For fresh herbs, 1:3. Example: 25g dried lavender in 100ml glycerin. Add 25ml distilled water to thin it (optional). Heat gently in a double boiler at 60Â°C for 2â3 hours. Or cold macerate for 4â6 weeks, shaking daily. Strain. Bottle. Shelf life: 1â2 years. Glycerites are less potent than tinctures but gentler. Use 1â2 teaspoons in 100ml water for a toner.

Safety: Alcohol tinctures are not for internal use unless you know the plant. For skincare, they are applied diluted. Glycerites can be used directly on skin but may be sticky. Always label with plant, solvent, ratio, and date. Store in cool, dark place. In hot climates, keep in fridge to extend life. You can combine tincture and glycerite for a custom extract. Test on a small skin patch before full use.

lessons.title: Steam Distillation for Hydrosols
lessons.body:
Steam distillation produces hydrosols (floral waters) and essential oils. Hydrosols are gentle, water-based, and perfect for toners, face mists, and creams. You can build a simple still at home using a large pot, a steamer basket or colander, a lid inverted, and a bowl to collect. Or buy a copper or stainless steel still. In Africa, you can use a pressure cooker with a copper tube if you are careful.

Basic method: Place 200g fresh or 100g dried plant material in the pot. Add water to just below the plant. Bring to a boil. Steam carries the plant oils. The steam hits a cold surface (lid with ice on top) and condenses. It drips into a bowl. Collect 200â500ml hydrosol. Example: 200g fresh rose petals gives about 300ml rose water. For lavender, use 150g dried flowers. Distill for 1â2 hours. Do not boil dry. Keep the heat steady.

Hydrosols are delicate. Store in sterilised dark glass bottles in the fridge. Shelf life: 6â12 months if refrigerated. Without fridge, 2â3 months. Add 1% preservative (like Geogard or potassium sorbate) for longer shelf life if selling. Use hydrosol directly as a toner or mix with glycerin (10ml glycerin per 100ml hydrosol) for a moisturising mist. For a face mask, mix 2 tablespoons clay with 1 tablespoon hydrosol.

Essential oil: If you want essential oil, you need a separator funnel. The oil floats on top. Collect it separately. Yield is very low: 200g lavender gives about 1â2ml oil. Use essential oils at 1â2% in skincare. Hydrosols are safer for direct use. Always label with plant and date. In Africa, good plants for distillation: rose, lavender, rosemary, eucalyptus, lemongrass, mint, chamomile. Avoid distilling poisonous plants. Clean your still thoroughly after each use.

lessons.title: Making Herbal Extracts with Alcohol
lessons.body:
Alcohol extracts (tinctures) are the most efficient for many herbs. They pull out resins, alkaloids, and volatile oils. For skincare, alcohol tinctures are used as preservatives, astringents, and active ingredients. You need strong alcohol: minimum 40% ABV (80 proof). Vodka is ideal. In Africa, you can use cane spirit, waragi, or even pure ethanol diluted to 40â60% with distilled water. Never use denatured alcohol or methylated spirits on skin.

Method: Measure dried herb. Use a 1:5 ratio (1 part herb to 5 parts alcohol by weight). For fresh herb, 1:2. Example: 20g dried rosemary in 100ml vodka. Chop herb coarsely. Place in a glass jar. Pour alcohol over. Seal. Shake well. Store in a dark cupboard for 4â6 weeks. Shake daily. Strain through muslin or coffee filter. Squeeze the herb to get all liquid. Bottle in dark glass with dropper. Label with plant, alcohol percentage, and date. Shelf life: 2â3 years.

For a stronger extract, use 60â70% alcohol for resins and barks. For delicate flowers, use 40â50%. You can also make a double extraction: first alcohol, then water decoction, and combine. This is good for mushrooms and tough roots. Example: 30g dried neem bark in 150ml 60% alcohol. Macerate 6 weeks. Strain. Use 5â10 drops in 30ml carrier oil for acne-prone skin.

Safety: Alcohol tinctures are for external use unless you are trained. They can sting on broken skin. Always dilute: 10â20 drops per 30ml of carrier oil or cream. For a facial toner, mix 10ml tincture with 90ml water or hydrosol. Store away from heat and light. In hot climates, keep in a cool cupboard. Do not use plastic bottles for long storage; glass is best. Test on a small area before using widely. Label everything. Keep out of reach of children.

lessons.title: Preserving Extracts for Longevity
lessons.body:
Preservation stops mould, bacteria, and rancidity. Water-based extracts (infusions, decoctions, hydrosols) spoil fastest: 2â7 days in the fridge. Oil-based extracts last 6â12 months. Alcohol and glycerin extracts last 1â3 years. The key is to prevent water from getting into oils and to keep everything clean.

For water extracts: Refrigerate immediately. Freeze in ice cube trays for up to 3 months. Add preservatives if selling: 1% Geogard 221 or 0.5% potassium sorbate plus 0.5% sodium benzoate. For hydrosols, add 1% preservative and store in dark glass in the fridge. For tinctures and glycerites, no preservative needed if alcohol or glycerin content is high enough. Alcohol above 20% prevents microbial growth. Glycerin above 50% also preserves. Always use sterilised bottles: boil glass for 10 minutes or wash with hot soapy water and rinse with alcohol.

For oil infusions: Add 1% vitamin E oil (tocopherol) to prevent rancidity. Store in dark glass bottles in a cool, dark place. Avoid sunlight. If you see cloudiness or smell off, discard. For balms and salves, the beeswax and oil mixture lasts 6â12 months. Add 0.5% rosemary oleoresin for extra protection. In hot African climates, keep oils in a cool box or fridge if possible. Never mix water into oil without an emulsifier and preservative; it will grow mould in days.

General rules: Label everything with plant name, extraction method, date, and expiry. Use clean utensils. Work with dry hands. Keep a notebook. Make small batches. If you sell, follow your country's regulations for cosmetics. Test preservative efficacy if possible. For home use, the fridge is your best friend. When in doubt, throw it out. Mould can cause skin infections. Proper preservation means your hard work lasts and your customers stay safe.

quiz.q: Which plant part is best suited for a cold infusion?
quiz.explanation: Cold infusion is used for delicate plant parts like flowers and leaves to avoid damaging their compounds.

quiz.q: What is the recommended ratio of dried herb to water for a decoction?
quiz.explanation: A standard decoction uses 30g of dried tough plant material to 500ml water.

quiz.q: How long should a cold infusion typically steep?
quiz.explanation: Cold infusions are left at room temperature for 4â8 hours or overnight to extract delicate compounds.

quiz.q: Why should you not use fresh herbs for solar oil infusion?
options: B) They contain water and cause mould
quiz.explanation: Fresh herbs contain water, which can lead to mould growth in oil infusions.

quiz.q: What temperature range is recommended for the heat method of oil infusion?
quiz.explanation: The heat method uses a double boiler at 60â70Â°C to gently extract without degrading the oil or herbs.

quiz.q: How long should a solar oil infusion sit?
quiz.explanation: Solar infusion typically takes 2â4 weeks in a sunny spot, shaking daily.

quiz.q: What is the correct ratio for a tincture using dried herbs?
quiz.explanation: For dried herbs, the standard tincture ratio is 1 part herb to 5 parts alcohol by weight.

quiz.q: What minimum alcohol percentage is needed for a tincture?
quiz.explanation: A minimum of 40% alcohol (80 proof) is needed to effectively extract and preserve tinctures.

quiz.q: How long should a tincture macerate?
quiz.explanation: Tinctures are typically macerated for 4â6 weeks, shaking daily.

quiz.q: What is a glycerite?
quiz.explanation: A glycerite uses vegetable glycerin as the solvent instead of alcohol.

quiz.q: What is the typical shelf life of a glycerite?
quiz.explanation: Glycerites have a shelf life of 1â2 years if stored properly.

quiz.q: In steam distillation, what is the water-based product called?
quiz.explanation: The water-based product of steam distillation is called a hydrosol or floral water.

quiz.q: How much hydrosol can you expect from 200g fresh rose petals?
quiz.explanation: About 300ml of hydrosol is typical from 200g fresh rose petals.

quiz.q: What is the shelf life of a hydrosol stored in the fridge?
quiz.explanation: Refrigerated hydrosols last 6â12 months; without refrigeration, 2â3 months.

quiz.q: What percentage of essential oil is safe for skincare?
quiz.explanation: Essential oils should be diluted to 1â2% in skincare products.

quiz.q: Which of these is a good plant for distillation in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Rose, lavender, and lemongrass are all suitable for distillation in Africa.

quiz.q: What type of alcohol is best for making herbal tinctures?
quiz.explanation: Vodka (40% ABV) is ideal; denatured, isopropyl, and methanol are toxic.

quiz.q: What is the ratio for a tincture using fresh herbs?
quiz.explanation: Fresh herbs require a 1:2 ratio (1 part herb to 2 parts alcohol) due to their water content.

quiz.q: How long does a typical alcohol tincture last?
quiz.explanation: Alcohol tinctures have a shelf life of 2â3 years if stored properly.

quiz.q: What is a double extraction?
options: C) First alcohol, then water decoction combined
quiz.explanation: A double extraction combines an alcohol tincture and a water decoction for maximum extraction.

quiz.q: What is the maximum time water-based extracts can be kept in the fridge?
quiz.explanation: Water-based extracts like infusions and decoctions spoil quickly, lasting 2â7 days in the fridge.

quiz.q: How can you extend the shelf life of a water extract without preservatives?
options: B) Freeze in ice cube trays
quiz.explanation: Freezing in ice cube trays extends shelf life up to 3 months.

quiz.q: What preservative can be added to water-based extracts for sale?
quiz.explanation: Geogard 221 is a broad-spectrum preservative for water-based cosmetics.

quiz.q: What minimum alcohol concentration prevents microbial growth in tinctures?
quiz.explanation: Alcohol above 20% prevents microbial growth in tinctures.

quiz.q: How should you sterilise glass bottles for extracts?
quiz.explanation: Boiling glass for 10 minutes sterilises bottles for safe storage.

quiz.q: What can you add to oil infusions to prevent rancidity?
quiz.explanation: Vitamin E oil (tocopherol) is an antioxidant that prevents oil rancidity.

quiz.q: What is the shelf life of a balm made with beeswax and infused oil?
quiz.explanation: Beeswax and oil balms last 6â12 months if stored properly.

quiz.q: Why should you never mix water into oil without an emulsifier and preservative?
quiz.explanation: Water in oil without preservative creates a breeding ground for mould and bacteria.

quiz.q: What should you label on every extract bottle?
quiz.explanation: Always label plant name, extraction method, date, and expiry for safety and tracking.

quiz.q: What is the best storage condition for most herbal extracts?
quiz.explanation: Cool, dark conditions preserve extracts best, except water-based ones that need refrigeration.
